title: How does @Column control field-to-column mapping, and what is the difference between JPA @Transient and the Java transient keyword?
keyPoints: @Column tunes field-to-column mapping: name, nullable, length, precision/scale, unique, insertable, updatable, and columnDefinition.
For money always use precision and scale on a BigDecimal (e.g., precision=15, scale=2), never length.
updatable=false prevents the column from appearing in UPDATE statements, perfect for createdAt timestamps.
JPA @Transient excludes a field from DATABASE mapping; the field is not persisted to any column.
Java transient keyword excludes a field from JAVA serialization only; it does NOT affect JPA mapping.
Confusing the two is a common bug: the keyword does not exclude from the database, only the annotation does.

s1_definition.oneliner: @Column tunes name, nullability, length, precision/scale, uniqueness, and insert/update inclusion; JPA @Transient excludes from the database, Java transient excludes from serialization.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@Column** – fine-tunes how an entity field maps to a database column: name, nullable, length, precision, scale, unique, updatable, insertable, and columnDefinition.
- **precision/scale** – for BigDecimal money fields, precision is the total number of digits, scale is the number after the decimal point (e.g., DECIMAL(15,2)).
- **updatable=false** – excludes the column from generated UPDATE statements, so the value is set once on INSERT and never changed.
- **JPA @Transient** – tells the persistence provider not to map the field to any column; the field is excluded from all SQL.
- **Java transient keyword** – tells Java's built-in Serializable mechanism to skip the field during object serialization; it has nothing to do with JPA.
- **Common confusion** – the Java transient keyword does NOT exclude a field from the database; only the JPA @Transient annotation does.
s1_definition.analogy: @Column is the instruction sheet telling the bank's filing clerk at National Bank of India exactly which box each piece of customer data goes into, how long the box can be, and whether the box is allowed to be empty. JPA @Transient is a sticky note saying this scratch calculation does NOT get filed in the vault at all, like a derived total you compute on screen but never store. Java's transient keyword is a totally different note that only matters when you photocopy the whole file to send elsewhere (serialization), telling the photocopier to leave that field blank.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @Column Attributes
  ============================================

  @Column(
    name = "holder_name",    -> column name in DDL
    nullable = false,        -> NOT NULL constraint
    length = 100,            -> VARCHAR(100)
    precision = 15,          -> DECIMAL total digits
    scale = 2,               -> DECIMAL decimal places
    unique = true,           -> UNIQUE constraint
    updatable = false,       -> excluded from UPDATE SQL
    insertable = false,      -> excluded from INSERT SQL
    columnDefinition = "TEXT" -> raw DDL type override
  )

  JPA @Transient vs Java transient
  ============================================

  Field: displayTotal
  +---------------------+
  | @Transient          |  -> NOT in database (no column)
  | (JPA annotation)    |  -> NOT in INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT
  +---------------------+  -> still in Jackson JSON

  Field: sessionCache
  +---------------------+
  | transient           |  -> NOT in ObjectOutputStream
  | (Java keyword)      |  -> STILL in database (has column!)
  +---------------------+  -> still in Jackson JSON

  Field: scratch
  +---------------------+
  | @Transient          |  -> NOT in database
  | + transient         |  -> NOT in ObjectOutputStream
  | (both)              |  -> excluded from BOTH
  +---------------------+
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The @Column annotation lets Rajesh control exactly how an entity field maps to a database column at National Bank of India. He sets the column name to bridge camelCase fields to snake_case columns, nullable=false to add a NOT NULL constraint, precision and scale for exact money storage, and updatable=false for timestamps that must never change after creation. For money he always uses precision=15, scale=2 on a BigDecimal, never length, so a balance maps to DECIMAL(15,2) which stores rupees and paise exactly without floating-point rounding.

The transient distinction is a classic interview trap and a real bug source. JPA @Transient means the field is not persistent at all, excluded from every SQL statement. The Java transient keyword is completely unrelated to JPA: it only tells Java's built-in serialization to skip the field, and it has no effect on database mapping or Jackson JSON. If Rajesh wants a field kept out of the database, he must use the JPA @Transient annotation. A field can carry both when he wants it out of both the database and Java serialization.

The senior cautions Pankaj gives are to always use the annotation rather than the keyword for excluding fields from persistence, to use precision and scale rather than length for money, and to keep annotations consistently on fields to avoid mixed field-and-property access surprises.

Remember one sentence: @Column tunes name, nullability, precision, and updatability for column mapping, while JPA @Transient excludes from the database and Java transient excludes from serialization.
